concepts.def: A fundamental particle (up, down, strange, charm, top, bottom) that makes up hadrons.
A fundamental particle not subject to the strong interaction; includes the electron, muon and neutrinos.
A composite particle made of quarks; subdivided into baryons (3 quarks) and mesons (quark-antiquark).
Boson mediating a fundamental force, e.g. photon (EM), W/Z (weak), gluon (strong).
A neutron decays to a proton, electron and antineutrino: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄_e.
In particle interactions, charge, baryon number, lepton number and energy/momentum are conserved.

Momentum, Nuclear & Particle Physics — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between nuclear fission and fusion?
options: Fission and fusion are the same process, just at different scales.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.

mcqs.q: In a collision between two objects, what quantity is always conserved (in a closed system)?
options: Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions because energy is conserved.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
Total momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.
Only the total mass in kilograms needs to balance.

mcqs.q: In a balanced nuclear equation, what must be equal on both sides?
options: Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.
Only the total mass in kilograms needs to balance.
The total mass number (top numbers) and the total atomic number (bottom numbers) must both balance.
Only the atomic number (proton count) needs to balance.
